iphone-loading-patterns.text:
iPhone loading — proposal, no product implementation

Boards: HomeLoadingPhone, ProjectsLoadingPhone, TaskLoadingPhone and LiveLoadingPhone show first loads at 390 × 844. HomeLoadingSlowPhone shows the same Work request after 10 seconds. HomeRefreshingPhone shows a foreground update over cached rows. HomeUnavailablePhone shows a failed connection with no disk cache; OfflinePhone remains the cached offline pattern. The last three are state variants, not additional destinations.

First load: use skeletons only for the requested resource when neither disk cache nor in-memory data exists. Keep the actual header, Back/Done, selected tab and known section names. Unknown names, counts, timestamps, health and computer labels are skeletons, never zero, “online”, “Healthy” or an empty state. Skeleton counts illustrate row geometry, not promised records. Reveal each independently loaded section when it is ready. Only a successful empty response may show the existing empty state, onboarding, zero count or “Unavailable” value. A failed request is a failure, never an empty response. Skeletons are static neutral .dl-skel shapes in the real row/message layout; no page spinner, shimmer, pulse or fake agent activity. Use the same still shapes with Reduce Motion.

Calm update over saved rows: show the cache immediately at full contrast. On opening or returning to a screen, reconnecting, or an explicit refresh, place the static, muted “Updating…” in the existing empty center header slot (HomeRefreshingPhone) as soon as the request starts, with no delay. When the request succeeds, replace it in that same slot with “Updated just now” and keep the timestamp until leaving the screen, so the line never flashes away; do not show a success toast. The timestamp may age to “Updated 1 min ago”. Do not move rows or the large title, hide readable data, disable navigation, or mark cached values as current until confirmed. Pull-to-refresh keeps its native gesture feedback; this line is the only additional refresh indicator. Automatic background polling changes data quietly and never starts this line, motion, shimmer or a completion message. A pending foreground request can update its existing line even if a background poll also finishes. Cancel/reset status on navigation and ignore responses for a previously opened resource.

After 10 seconds: name the resource still pending, not a generic “Loading”. Work: “Work is taking longer than usual to load from SER.” Secondary: “Still trying. Your work will appear here when it arrives.” Projects: “Projects are taking longer than usual to load from SER.” Task or agent chat: “This conversation is taking longer than usual to load from SER.” Live: “App status is taking longer than usual to load from SER.” Use the same warning banner above the affected section with “Still trying.” for the secondary line on other destinations. Keep partial results. Over cached rows use this same banner, retain readable rows, and replace the header’s Updating with “Waiting for SER…”. Do not restart the 10-second clock on each retry or poll. Announce status changes once, not on every skeleton row or poll; keep navigation outside aria-busy and hide decorative skeletons from accessibility.

Unreachable: replace the pending/slow state as soon as the request is known to have failed; do not wait for 10 seconds or leave skeletons animating forever. With cached rows, reuse OfflinePhone’s warning, last-known labels and dimmed data exactly; existing offline read/write behavior is unchanged. Without cache, HomeUnavailablePhone says “Can't reach SER” / “Retrying. No saved work on this iPhone.”, offers Try now, and says “Check that this iPhone is on the same network as SER.” Keep navigation; show neither a last-heard timestamp nor fake empty content. Apply resource-specific copy elsewhere: “No saved projects on this iPhone.”, “No saved conversation on this iPhone.” or “No saved app status on this iPhone.” Try now retries the missing resource; success restores content, another failure retains the notice. No new offline send/queue behavior is proposed.

Coverage of the rest of the audit (same patterns, no extra boards):
• Home Agents and Waiting on you: independent HomeLoadingPhone groups, never empty before the respective response.
• Answered: ProjectsLoadingPhone grouped rows; “No answered decisions” only after success. Slow: “Answered decisions are taking longer than usual to load from SER.”
• Computers: LiveLoadingPhone computer rows with skeleton summary and status; no “0 online” before success. Slow: “Computers are taking longer than usual to load from SER.”
• Project detail: keep its known project title and navigation, use ProjectsLoadingPhone row geometry in each actual section; do not invent app/release tabs before their data establishes they exist. Slow: “Project details are taking longer than usual to load from SER.”
• App detail: LiveLoadingPhone rows in the app’s actual summary layout; skeleton health/metrics until known. Slow: “App details are taking longer than usual to load from SER.”
• Backups and Paired devices: ProjectsLoadingPhone grouped rows within the existing page or sheet, preserve Done/Back. Slow: “Backups are taking longer than usual to load from SER.” / “Paired devices are taking longer than usual to load from SER.”
• Task chat and Agent chat: TaskLoadingPhone conversation lines; keep known title, tabs and local draft, do not show the agent’s onboarding card before a successful empty history. Sending waits until the destination is ready; this proposal does not change queuing. Changes and Checks load independently in their existing row layouts, never “No changes yet” / “No checks yet” while pending. Slow: “Changes are taking longer than usual to load from SER.” / “Checks are taking longer than usual to load from SER.”
• Settings approvals: skeleton agent summary rows and permission values in the existing groups. “No agents” requires success; “Unavailable” is for a confirmed unavailable capability, not a request still pending. Slow: “Approvals are taking longer than usual to load from SER.”
• Agent info / learned details: skeleton only the unknown fields and learned rows in the existing sheet; preserve any already known identity. Never “Nothing learned yet” before success. Slow: “Agent details are taking longer than usual to load from SER.”
• Agent runs: ProjectsLoadingPhone grouped run rows; “No runs yet” only after success. Slow: “Agent runs are taking longer than usual to load from SER.”
• Packages: replace the page spinner with skeleton package rows in the existing Private and Copies sheet groups. Load the two parts independently as PackagesPhone already specifies; preserve one part when the other is pending or fails. Never fabricate storage zero or registry reachability. Slow per section: “Private packages are taking longer than usual to load from SER.” / “Package copies are taking longer than usual to load from SER.”
• Package versions: skeleton version/date rows inside the existing versions sheet; keep the known package title and Done. Slow: “Package versions are taking longer than usual to load from SER.”
• Design and Releases: keep their existing skeleton row layout as the reference pattern; add the same per-resource slow, cache-refresh and failure rules. Slow: “Design is taking longer than usual to load from SER.” / “Releases are taking longer than usual to load from SER.”

All other cached destinations follow HomeRefreshingPhone; all other failures follow the cache/no-cache split above with the resource named in the notice. No product code, new empty-state copy or new navigation is authorized by these boards. Owner decision: Updating… appears with no delay. The foreground-only rule and the persistent “Updated just now” timestamp are proposed to make arrivals visible without polling motion or flicker.

app-performance.text:
Second waterfall pass, design only; owner approval pending. Requests retains app totals and its request log. Route lists keep one segmented p50 server bar per route on a shared scale: Forma 0–100 ms, Medius 0–200 ms, compendus 0–20 ms. Thin marker: total route p95. Stable colors everywhere, using existing light/dark tokens: route match accent, data loading success, page render warning, streaming active. Browser milestones use neutral ink-soft. Each routes list and each timing part/comparison has a wrapping legend. Lighter extensions use the same phase color at 30% opacity.

Opened routes split into On the server and In the browser, each with its own axis. Server axes match the app's route-list scale. Server phases begin at the previous typical phase's end, solid through p50 with a lighter extension to the phase p95 duration from that same start. Those per-phase percentiles cannot be added to make one p95 request. Forma /watch/:id uses 0.1 + 18 + 9 + 7 = 34.1 ms on 0–100 ms; its streaming extension ends at 72.9 ms. Browser bars run from navigation start to each milestone on 0–5 s. /watch/:id milestones: 82 ms, 1.1 s, 4.3 s. Unknown Interactive rows are omitted; never substitute INP or zero. One plain note per timing part, with no percentile/clock jargon on screen.

Data the build will provide: p50/p95 per phase per route; a small sample of the slowest requests per route per hour with their phases; browser milestones linked to a sampled request by a request ID. Route browser percentiles use only linked samples; Page experience remains the separate p75 visit population. A minimum 1 px mark preserves subpixel route-match phases without changing numeric offsets.

Slowest requests has normal section spacing and links to the exact request. AppPerformanceRequest and AppPerformanceRequestPhone default to forma-watch-127 (127 ms, 200, release a1b2c3d), with browser milestones including Interactive. Single requests have sequential server bars on 0–100/200/300 ms and navigation-based browser milestones on 0–6 s, containing the existing 5.2 s paint sample; no p95 tail. Default /watch/:id server offsets are 0, 0.1, 18.1, 27.1, 127 ms. AppPerformanceRequestNoBrowser draws the 143 ms / 502 sample, error Media source did not answer, as a second web board. Only that sample has the plain missing-report line. The phone keeps its fragment-selected 502 sample; API requests show only server phases. Other formerly missing page-sample browser fixtures reuse their route's linked-sample milestone values. All are static design fixtures, not runtime measurements. Surviving layers and all 27 request IDs remain.

Release and Waiting comparisons keep existing before/after data and now use the same phase colors/legend. No app, CLI, desktop or native implementation is authorized. Existing chrome, four ranges, ratings, empty/totals states, finding choices, counts, rollback scope and receipts remain. Phone overview links still demonstrate the existing /watch/:id route fixture. Rendering at 1440/700 and 390, dark theme, phone scrolling and before/after captures belong to the orchestrator; this sandbox cannot launch Chromium.

app-performance-thresholds.text:
Page-experience ratings use browser visits at p75 per route. Good / Needs work / Poor use the standard inclusive boundaries: LCP ≤2.5 s / ≤4 s / >4 s; INP ≤200 ms / ≤500 ms / >500 ms; CLS ≤0.1 / ≤0.25 / >0.25. First byte uses the separate TTFB guide ≤800 ms / ≤1,800 ms / >1,800 ms; it is not a Core Web Vital. Status is written out, with existing success/warning/danger text tokens, never a colored badge. No universal thresholds are invented for request response, navigation time, or prefetch hits.

Sources checked: https://web.dev/articles/defining-core-web-vitals-thresholds and https://web.dev/articles/ttfb . “Needs work” is the product's plain wording for “needs improvement”. Medius at 160 ms is a relative release regression, not a poor TTFB score. These boundaries apply to the rating list; linked-sample timing percentiles live in the waterfall.

Release rows compare the measured post-release period with the 24 hours immediately before release. Keep the baseline and post-release request counts visible in the regression evidence; these are unequal-duration populations. A current release is still being measured, not automatically healthy. Edge request errors are separate from grouped server, page, action and browser occurrences. Errors are grouped by fingerprint, retaining latest message/stack, all-time first/last seen, route, where, hourly range counts and releases.

Waterfall revision: p75 rating thresholds are unchanged, but largest paint and first byte numbers now live only in the route waterfall (linked-sample p50/p95). Rating words remain based on all measured browser visits at p75; the populations are explicitly different. Medius all-range server p50 remains 70 ms. Post-release / phases are 0.1 / 120 / 12 / 7.9 = 140 ms, versus 0.1 / 40 / 12 / 7.9 = 60 ms before release. The rest is steady; data loading grew 80 ms. Comparison bars share 0–200 ms and show p50 phases. Historical Forma 72bf901 compares /watch/:id data loading 10 → 18 ms, total ≈26 → 34 ms. Browser first byte 72 → 160 ms remains separate p75 evidence, not the server total.

app-performance-decisions.text:
AppPerformanceInbox / AppPerformanceInboxPhone copy the existing Inbox / WaitingCarePhone list and add a card among the other cards: Ops watcher avatar, Performance · medius, title, one line of evidence and the ordinary Review finding action link. The existing five-proposal capacity notice is unchanged: the performance finding is an operational decision, not a sixth care proposal. The web list is eight waiting decisions rather than seven.

Review finding opens AppPerformanceWaiting / AppPerformanceWaitingPhone in the existing care detail pattern: title, agent kind line, explanation, evidence and one set of decision buttons. Keep first byte before/now, errors before/now, since release, baseline/request counts and p75. Look at it opens Medius performance and leaves the finding waiting. Roll back… opens whole-project review naming Medius and Medius jobs and the absence of migrations. It’s fine retains 6d7e8f9 and records who/when/device in Answered. No second choices list. Phone evidence scrolls above the existing care footer.

Rollback approval records rolling back, not recovery. The local #approved target hides decision controls and only Medius’s waiting row; the other three sidebar items remain, with their original times. The count returns from four to three. Health results must return on the same item. No new rule, suppression or numerical trigger is introduced. Owner approval is pending; these are design-only revisions, left uncommitted for the orchestrator. No server, deployment, real data or product implementation.

Waterfall revision: put two thin before/after server bars on the Medius regression, its slower release and the opened Waiting on you finding, preserving choices, counts and rollback semantics. Evidence labels name / and data loading 40 → 120 ms; before 60 ms, after 140 ms. Existing p75 first-byte and error evidence remains. Forma historical slower release gets a /watch/:id phase comparison as well.

app-performance-capture.text:
Orchestrator capture required: this sandbox must not launch Chromium, Electron, Xcode or Simulator. Boards are standalone file URLs; no fixture server command is needed. Render the changed/new boards using the exact command in docs/evidence/app-performance-design/README.md: 6 changed/new web × 2 widths (1440, 700) + 7 phone at 390 = 19 initial PNGs. Use 1ad36267 as Before; for new request boards use the previous route detail as context, clearly labelled new screen. Show one before/after pair in the owner conversation and propose for explicit design approval before implementation.

Inspect shared list-scale bars, p95 markers and phase tooltip labels; open every web route disclosure and scroll to its 3 slow samples. Inspect the long seconds axis on /watch/:id, p95 extensions, duration labels, Unavailable Interactive and no browser rows on the API route. Scroll phone Route to Waterfall, Slowest requests and Page experience; scroll all overview phone bodies to ratings, errors and releases. Follow all request links; capture default #forma-watch-143 and #forma-watch-127 (browser milestones), plus Medius and quiet request fragments. No duplicated largest-paint/first-byte timings in ratings. Check before/after bars in both releases and Waiting, including fixed phone footer and all 3 choices. Confirm totals-only one-line note, narrow range controls and unchanged chrome. New shared dl-waterfall primitive uses existing tokens and dl-bar/list components; no new palette or type sizes.

project-way-back.text: Getting back from a project. Every page inside a project starts its header with a breadcrumb: Projects, then the project. An app page in a project with several apps adds the app; a one-app project stops at the project, because the project is the app. The current page is not a link. Tabs stay siblings and never appear in the breadcrumb. Going back to Projects, by the breadcrumb, the sidebar or browser Back, returns to the same place in the list. In the desktop app, View also has Back (⌘[) and Forward (⌘]). On iPhone a project opens as its own page, with the back button and swipe, and no longer unfolds below the list.

review-what-changed.text:
Design review is one surface. The bar holds the proposal, Before and After, the screen width and the decision. The list on the left is what changed, not every screen: screens with the same change are one row, with the words and “Nothing else changed on these screens”. A screen joins a group only if nothing else on it differs. The rest of the page is the real design at its real size, the change outlined.
A floating toolbar stays on the design. Its tools are select, pin a point, mark an area and draw; pick one and use it on the design, and the note appears there, with no tray. Beside them is one scrubber from Old to New. In Overlay it fades the old screen over the new one, so what moved doubles up and what stayed stays sharp; in Wipe it drags a divider across the two. The choice is remembered. A row counts once as looked at. Left and Right walk every screen in order, carrying on from one change into the next; Up and Down jump a whole change. The keys stop at either end.
The screen has no fixed sizes. It opens fitted to the window, and dragging its edge sets any width, with the width shown while dragging. Boards are live HTML, so the design reflows and the outlines follow it. A note is tied to the element under it, so it stays put at any width. A phone screen opens at its own width; on iPhone, pinch to zoom.
Decide in the same bar. Approve is the main action with no notes; with notes, Send is. Approving with a note not sent asks first. Approving waits 30 seconds, then goes to main; Undo stops it. The decision stays where it was made: the bar reads Approved with the check and the countdown, and a dashed record tops the list with who, when and where. Once it is on main the record gives the commit, Undo gives way to Next review (Done when nothing else waits), and the foot says what happens now: the proposer’s task with Open the task, or “Nothing builds this yet” with Start a task when you proposed it yourself. A link change that looks the same reads “looks the same”. “Nothing else changed” is said only when the rendered pixels outside the outlines match. If pixels differ with no changed element, the row reads “Looks different; no element changed” and the whole screen shows.
Proposing asks what it is and what changed and why, and agents must send both. To review keeps approved work: being built, built and matching, or built with a difference.

design-build-check.text:
Closing the loop on an approved design. Approving a design puts it on main and starts nothing; you ask for the build from the approved review on the canvas or in the proposer’s chat (see build-on-ask).
• A task linked to an approved design gets an Approved design check on its Checks tab: Matches the approved design. Until the builder reports, the header reads Design not checked, Merge and release is off, and More offers Merge without the design check.
• The builder renders each changed board, captures the app at the same widths and reports matches or differs. Matches turns the check green and the task can read Ready to merge. Compare opens the pairs.
• Differs brings one item to Waiting on you with the design and the app side by side at the width that differs, what differs and why. Fix the app sends it back to the same task. Keep it and update the design passes the check as Kept and has the builder change the board in the same task to match the app; that answer is its approval, and the board lands with the merge. No third choice; Open the task is a link.
• A task with no approved design shows none of this.

sidebar-quiet.text:
The sidebar is quiet until there is something to show.
• Order: New task and the places, then Waiting on you, Agents, Today and earlier days.
• A section appears with its first item. Nothing waiting: no Waiting on you row and no 0. No agents: one row, New agent, in place of the heading and the sentence. No tasks today: no Today heading.
• Waiting on you sits under the places, not above them, so the places never move as decisions come and go.
• Agents are one line each: avatar, name, time. The last message shows on hover and in the agent’s chat.
• Search stays out of the app until it works; a disabled “coming soon” button is an empty state too.

phone-review-tools.text:
iPhone review: one bar of tools, and the screen gets the room.
• The bottom area was a third of the screen: three lines of words, a slider, a row of tools, two labels and a progress bar. It is now one line of words and one bar.
• The bar, left to right: Previous screen; Pin, Mark an area, Draw; Compare, Fit; Next screen. Every target is at least 40 × 44 pt. Swiping still moves between screens when the screen is fitted or untouched.
• Compare shows the Old to New scrubber and stays on until tapped again; its button is highlighted meanwhile. Upright, the scrubber sits above the bar; sideways, it floats at the bottom middle. The chip at its end switches Overlay and Wipe. The scrubber is hidden otherwise (DesignReviewComparingPhone, DesignReviewLandscapeComparingPhone).
• Fit switches between the whole screen in view and real size, the same as double-tap. “Pinch to zoom” is no longer written on screen.
• The words are one line: what changed, then “1 of 4” for the change. Tapping it opens the full words in a sheet. The thin line above is the position in the review; the header keeps “22 of 28”.
• Turned sideways the screen fills the window. The header becomes a small pill at the top left (Back, name, position) and the bar stands on the right edge with the same tools in the same order. No words line; they open from the pill.
• The other iPhone review boards (draw, pin, compare, new screen) still show the old bottom area and follow once this is approved.

task-needs-computer.text:
A task says what it needs, and the computers answer.
• No list to maintain: a project does not declare what its folders need, and nobody tags computers.
• Nothing is built in about which work needs which tool. The agent works it out from the request and the repository and states the tools it needs by the name of the program it will run (xcodebuild, docker, swift), as its first step. A build started by approving a design is no different: its agent reads the approved boards and says what it needs. You can state a need yourself on the composer’s computer chip.
• deploy.local asks every computer that takes tasks whether it has each one. A computer answers by looking for that program there and then, so any program can be asked about and the answer is never stale. An answer is remembered for a computer that is offline.
• With one that qualifies online, the task starts there and nothing looks different. With none, the task waits with one banner: what it needs, who was asked and what they said, and that nothing has run. Choose a computer overrides it.
• An agent can find a need partway (the tests need Docker). It says so, the task pauses at its checkpoint, and the same ask happens: Move to a computer that has it, as on TaskStalled.
• Waiting for a computer is not a decision: no attention glyph, not in Waiting on you.
• A design check is only accepted from a computer that has what the task said it needs.
• Computers shows what each computer has answered so far on its row.

sidebar-instances.text:
The sidebar is one component. Every board holds an instance of Sidebar from the library (Assets › Navigation), not a copy of its markup.
• Change the sidebar by changing the component: approving that change redraws every board.
• An instance’s settings say what this board shows: the window (browser, Mac window, with the collapse button), the selected place or row, the Live summary, which decisions wait, whether there are agents, the current task and how full Today is, and the account line.
• The fixture is the same everywhere: the same three decisions, five agents and four tasks. A board adds at most two decisions and one task of its own. The count beside Waiting on you is the number of rows shown.
• The five Mac update boards put the update card inside the sidebar and keep their own markup.
• A test fails when a board copies the sidebar instead of placing it, or falls out of step with the library.
• Next to convert, by how often they repeat and how far the copies have drifted: the page header bar (177 boards, 33 different structures), the phone top bar (126, 27), tabs (66, 29), the composers (web 39, phone 41), the phone tab bar (34), the approval card (24), the task header (16, 11 structures) and the This task panel (15).

resolve-conflicts.text:
A conflict is resolved in the review, not handed back.
• A proposal conflicts when main has changed a screen it also changes. The review opens on those screens first, under Changed on main too, before the changes.
• Different parts of a screen: both are kept, automatically. The row says Kept both and what each side changed. Nothing to choose, and such a screen never blocks the review. Parts are elements of the board, not lines of its file.
• The same part: the row shows what main has and what the proposal has, and two answers under it: Keep main’s or Keep this proposal’s. The screen beside it scrubs between Main and This proposal with the same tool that compares Old and New.
• Each answer is undoable until you approve. Continue review turns on when every screen is resolved, and the changes follow as usual. Approving then puts the resolved screens on main.
• Ask to update stays, as the quiet action, for a conflict that needs real rework. When an agent proposed the design it goes to its task. When you proposed it yourself, it starts a task to do the update; it never goes nowhere.
• iPhone: the same, one conflicting screen per page, with the two answers in place of the tool bar. A conflict opens without waiting for the other screens to draw.
• Canvas notes conflict the same way: both kept when they changed different notes, a choice when they changed the same one.

app-performance-as-built.text:
Performance as it ships on the web, approved by the owner on November 11, 2026 as a smaller first page.
• Ranges are 1 hour, 24 hours and 7 days.
• A route opens to its server phases. Phase bars appear for traffic measured after this ships; older traffic has totals only.
• Not built yet, and off these boards until SER serves them: 30 days, the in-browser timeline, slowest requests and the single-request page (AppPerformanceRequest boards), an error’s hourly count and the releases it was seen in.
• The finding in Waiting on you and the iPhone screens are not built either; their boards are unchanged.

chart-hover-logs-status.text:
For approval. Two small answers to “what am I looking at?”
• Requests chart: pointing at it reads that minute. A line marks the minute, a dot sits on each series, and the legend row says the time, requests a minute and server errors in place of the peak. Moving off brings the peak back. Touch: drag across the chart. Keyboard: focus the chart, then Left and Right.
• Logs says what its stream is doing. Connecting while it opens, Live while lines can arrive, Disconnected with Reconnect when it stops. “Paused” goes away: nothing was paused. A read that fails keeps its banner and Retry.

phone-app-logs-settings.text:
For approval. iPhone gets an app’s Logs and Settings, so its app page has the same places as the web one.
• The app page lists Releases, Logs and Settings under App.
• Logs are the app’s own lines as it writes them, newest at the bottom, wrapped to the screen. Filter by text or level. Live says the stream is open. From a project, the same screen shows every app, each line starting with its app’s name.
• Settings shows the address, the health check, where it runs and the memory limit, which can be changed here. Everything else is the project’s.
• Nothing here is new to the server: the phone reads what the web pages read.

health-default.text:
For approval. An app does not have to declare a health check to be watched.
• With no check declared, deploy.local asks the app’s own address: GET /. Any answer that is not a server error (below 500) is healthy, so a sign-in redirect counts. Live, the menu bar and the app page say “GET / 200” as they do for a declared check.
• A declared check keeps its stricter rule: it must answer 2xx.
• A release uses the same default for its gate before going live: the new copy must answer GET / where it used to only accept a connection.
• “Health checks unavailable” is left for an app with no address to ask, such as one that only listens on a raw port. A worker is still judged by its heartbeat and jobs.
• Failing still takes three missed checks in a row.

desktop-runs-worker.text:
For approval. The desktop app is the one place a computer’s worker is installed, changed, repaired and removed.
• Setup offers Run apps on any computer with Docker. Turning it on installs one background service, so apps keep running when the app is quit and start again after a restart. Take tasks still lives with the app.
• The menu bar says what this computer is doing. When it cannot reach its apps it says what is wrong in plain words and offers the fix: Restart Docker, or Repair the worker. Nobody opens a terminal to find out.
• A computer set up earlier from the command line is offered a move. Nothing changes until you accept. The computer keeps its name, its apps, their addresses and their ports. An older copy that needs a password to remove is named, not hidden.
• The terminal keeps one command, for a computer you cannot sit at: install and join with a code. The other deploy agent commands go away once every computer has moved.
• Not drawn here: Windows, and the Linux versions of these four screens (same content in the Linux window, as SetupLinux).

release-and-computer-stats.text:
For approval. deploy.local says where time goes, and when a computer is struggling.
• A release step lists its parts with their times: copy data, build image, send, first answer. A running step shows the part it is in and how long so far.
• A step on another computer is stopped only when that computer reports nothing for 10 minutes, not at a fixed 20. The release says when it last heard from it.
• A computer’s page shows how long its disk and Docker take to answer. When either is slow for several minutes the page says so in plain words, and a release running there links to it.
• Nothing here blocks a release; it only explains a slow one. Phones get the same step wording; the phone boards are unchanged in layout.

link-app-repository.text:
An app and its repository are one project

An app shipped from a folder has no repository. Its page says so and offers Add a repository (AppNoRepository, AddRepository); the same row sits in its Settings. The repository takes the app’s name and joins the app’s project, so the Projects list never shows the name twice. Afterwards the Code tab appears with the push commands from ProjectEmpty. The CLI keeps shipping from the folder until deploy.yaml is on main.

New project with the name of an app that has no repository adds the repository to that app (NewProjectExistingApp). A name no such app uses creates a project as before.

A repository with no app offers Add an app you shipped (ProjectEmpty, AddExistingApp). The dialog lists only apps with no repository, the one with the project’s name first, and replaces the dialog that asked you to type an app’s name. With no such app the link is not shown. Adding moves the app’s variables, secrets and releases into the project.

iPhone: later.

projects-and-live.text:
Projects and Live show the same things

A project is a repository, what it runs, or both. Projects lists every one of them, deployed first; Live lists the running ones by computer. Neither page has anything the other cannot name.

Projects: two groups, Live and Repositories. Live is a grid of cards, two across and one on a phone-width window, the ones that need you first. A card has the project’s initial, its name, where it runs (the address and computer for one app, “2 apps · SER and imac” for several, “Stopped 3 days ago” for one you stopped), its health, a line of today’s requests with the count under it, and at most one more fact: an open PR, a proposal, Maintained, or “Shipped from a folder”. Repositories is a list, newest change first: the repository, its last commit’s subject, and open PRs with when it changed. It shows six and “Show 9 more”, which fetches the next page; nothing below the first page is read until asked for.

Archived projects (the Done stage: app stopped, repository read-only, final backup kept) are hidden. The Show menu beside the filter has three ticks, Live, Repositories and Archived, any number at once; Live and Repositories start ticked, and the button names what is ticked (“Live and repositories”, “Archived”, “All projects”). The choice is remembered on this computer. Typing in Filter projects searches every project whatever is ticked, so an archived project you name still turns up, in an Archived group at the end.

Live: every row names its project and opens it. “No project” is gone, because an app shipped from a folder is a project of its own. Apps from Discover keep “From Discover”.

Both boards now use the same eight running apps. Live stays a page: the per-computer table, traffic and the alert card do not fit a project row.

iPhone: later. ProjectsRail keeps its older list; it only shows the rail.

review-on-canvas.text:
For approval: a review happens on the canvas

Reviewing a design opens the Design canvas on the proposal’s branch, not a separate review surface. Same frames, same panels, same tools.

• Changed and new frames stay at full strength, tagged Changed or New, with the changed areas marked on them. Everything else is dimmed. Before and After switches what the frames show.
• Each changed frame has a checkbox beside its name. Ticking it approves that frame. The bar counts them: 1 of 3 approved.
• The arrows in the tool bar, and ← →, move to the previous and next changed frame and zoom to it. Space ticks the frame you are on.
• Because it is the canvas, a reviewer can do more than write: comment on a layer, draw, or edit the frame. Those land on the branch as suggestions for the proposer.
• Links on a frame work as they do everywhere on the canvas, and the frame they open is right there beside it. There is nothing to go back from.
• Changes on this branch, in the right panel, is the list of what changed. The review’s own list, viewer and dock go away, and so does their code.
• Approve design is available at any time; unticked frames are named before it goes through. Ask for changes sends the comments, drawings and edits.

This replaced the one-surface DesignReview boards on web, which are retired. The states it has are drawn beside it: Approve, Ask for changes, Sent, approved with Undo, and Changed on main too. iPhone keeps its pager.

build-on-ask.text:
Approving a design does not start a build

Approving puts the design on main and stops there. No task starts on its own.

The canvas stays on the review, now approved: every changed frame ticked, and the bar reads Approved · on main as <commit> · not built yet. Ask for changes and Approve design give way to one button: Build.

• Build does the usual thing: it carries on in the task that proposed the design, so that conversation builds it. The approval also shows in that chat, where saying “build it” or pressing Build does the same.
• The arrow beside it chooses where: In <proposer>’s task, or In a new task. The choice is remembered for the next design. A design a person proposed has no task to carry on in, so Build starts a new task and there is no arrow.
• Nothing is timed. Build is there today or next week.

Once a task is building it the bar names who and links the task in place of “not built yet”, and the buttons go. The design check on that task works as before (design-build-check): the app is compared with the approved boards before it can merge.

This replaces “When the design lands on main its build starts” in design-build-check. iPhone: the approved page says Not built yet; building is started from web or the chat.

page-templates.text:
Page templates. A new feature picks one of four templates instead of drawing a layout: List (Projects), Detail (a project), Conversation (a task) and Settings (Settings), each on web and iPhone. They are components in the library (Assets › Page templates), placed as instances like the Sidebar, with settings for the words that change.
• Existing boards already follow them: List — Projects, Compute, AgentsEmpty, ProjectPhone, ComputePhone. Detail — Project, App, AgentSettings, ProjectDetailPhone, AppSettingsPhone. Conversation — Task, AgentPage, Home, TaskPhone, AgentPhone. Settings — Settings, SettingsAgents, ProjectSettings, SettingsPhone, SettingsApprovalsPhone.
• Those boards keep their own markup for now. Moving them onto the instances is a later step, one board at a time, once these are approved.
• In the app, each template becomes one page component; a feature supplies its rows and actions.

project-polish.text:
For approval. Four things that got in the way on a project.

Discover has a way back. Its header reads Projects › Discover, like every page under Projects, and the sidebar keeps Projects selected (Discover).

One settings page for a project with one app. Settings shows the app’s Address and Health and resources, then the project’s Variables and secrets, Repository and Releases, then Remove, on one page (OneAppSettings). There is no second page and no notice sending you to it. A project with several apps keeps Project settings, and each app’s address, health and limits stay on that app’s page under the project.

Pipelines on a narrow window. Below 820 px the run you are looking at sits on top as one full-width row that says how many runs there are; tapping it opens the list. Its jobs, packages and release follow directly, so nothing is a long scroll away. The tab row fades at its edge when more tabs follow, and the current tab is scrolled into view (PipelineRun at 700).

Numbers that are not there. “Unavailable” goes. When nothing happened the number is the truth: 0 requests per minute with “No requests in the last hour”, and a dash for a time with “No requests to time” (OneAppQuiet). When something is not measured the row says “Not measured” and why, for example “Traffic is not recorded for this app”. A memory limit that was never set reads “No limit”. Loading still shows a skeleton, never a zero.

iPhone: later.

work-9.text:
Tidying tasks
Web app · Desktop app
iPhone: later

tasks-group-delete.text:
Tasks in the sidebar group by date or by project; the first heading carries the choice and the app remembers it. By project: projects in order of their latest task, each with its 5 most recent tasks and “Show N more”; tasks with no project come last under No project. The + on a project starts a task in it.

Delete task… is in a row’s ⋯ (shown in place of the time on hover or keyboard focus, and on right-click in the desktop app) and in the task’s own ⋯ menu. It always asks first and names what goes: the conversation, its checkpoints and its branch. The notice appears only when the branch has commits that are not on main. An open pull request is closed; merged work and releases stay. While a task is running the item is absent: stop it first.

one-search.text:
One search, everywhere
• One box. The magnifier in the sidebar, ⌘K, a project’s Code tab and Search on iPhone all open it. There is no separate search page and no second search.
• Names first: projects, apps, tasks, agents, computers, packages, pull requests and issues match by name as you type.
• Text second, from three characters: lines of code, and messages in tasks and agent chats. Plain text, ignoring case.
• Opened inside a project, it starts in that project, shown as a token before the words; Backspace searches everywhere. Show all narrows to one kind the same way.
• Code is searched on each project’s main branch, or on the branch the Code tab is showing.
• A code result opens the file at that line, with every match marked. A message opens its chat at that message.
• Names never wait for code: the Code heading says Searching… until its lines arrive.
• The Code tab’s Go to file box becomes Search this project ( / ); file names are the first group there.

artifacts.text:
For approval: Design becomes Artifacts

The sidebar place Design is renamed Artifacts and opens a gallery of every project’s artifacts. A design is one kind of artifact; a document is the second. More kinds are added only when they exist.

• Make something new sits at the top: one tile per kind. A tile asks for a name and the project, then deploy.local creates the files on a new branch and opens it. Nobody adds canvas.json by hand.
• Below, one card per artifact with a preview, its project and when it last changed. A card says In review or Not proposed only while its newest work is not on main. All, Designs and Documents filter the cards.
• The grid is three cards wide at 1440 and two at 700.
• A project can hold several. Each lives in its own folder, artifacts/<name>, in the project’s repository. The design a project already has in design/ stays where it is and is listed as App design.
• Opening a design goes to the canvas. Review, Before and After, and approval onto main are unchanged and apply to every kind.
• On the canvas, the project menu’s line about design/canvas.json becomes New artifact.

• Create opens the new design’s canvas straight away: empty, on its own branch, with the tools ready and one button to ask an agent to start it.
• A document opens as a page under Artifacts, in the reading column. Edit starts a branch for it; proposing and approving work as they do for a design.

• On iPhone, Artifacts is a row in Settings beside Packages and opens as a sheet: Make something new first, then each project’s artifacts as rows. A design opens the canvas the phone already has.

• On the canvas, the menu at the top of the left panel lists designs, each with its project, and ends with New artifact. Projects with no design are no longer listed there. At narrow widths the bar reads Artifacts and goes back to the gallery.
• On iPhone a kind opens a short sheet: Name, Project, Cancel and Create.

• Editing a document is typing in the page. Edit starts a branch for it; the header then shows the branch, how many blocks changed and Propose. A small bar gives bold, italic, lists, link and code; Link asks for the address in the browser’s own prompt. Text styles are not drawn, so the bar has none. Each changed block gets a dot in the margin, and every edit is saved to the branch as you type.
• On iPhone a document opens in a sheet to read. Editing a document on iPhone is not drawn.

As built:
• The Document tile opens the same dialog, titled New document. When Create is refused, the reason shows under Name.
• Ask an agent on an empty canvas opens the ask box the canvas already has, headed with the design’s name.
• New artifact in the design menu goes to the gallery.
• On iPhone a document’s back button is the system chevron, and a project’s artifacts are listed newest first.

Reviewing a document:
• A proposed document opens on its own page under Artifacts, in the reading column, not on the canvas. The review bar from the design review sits at the top of the page: the proposal’s title, who it is from and how many blocks changed, then Before and After, Ask for changes and Approve document. Approving, undo and Ask for changes work as they do for a design.
• After shows the document as proposed, with a dot beside each block that is not on main. Before shows the document on main, with a dot beside each block the proposal changes or removes.
• A document that is not on main yet has no Before: Before is dimmed and cannot be chosen, the bar says new document, and no block has a dot.
• Wherever a document’s line would say on main while it is only on its branch, it says not on main yet: reading, editing and reviewing, on web and iPhone. A document on main that is being edited keeps its branch on that line.
• The approve action for a document reads Approve document everywhere Approve design would: Waiting on you, the review bar and iPhone.
• On iPhone a document review opens from Waiting on you as Document review: Before and After at the top, the document below, Approve document and Ask for changes at the bottom. Editing a document on iPhone is not drawn.
• A task that changes an artifact design gets the Design tab as it does for design/, and it opens that artifact’s review or canvas. A task that changes a document gets the tab once it is proposed, and it opens the document’s review.

Reviewing a document, as built:
• Approving and asking for changes on web use the design review’s dialogs, the 30-second undo and its Approved · on main line; a document has no Build.
• While a document not on main yet is edited, no block has a dot either.
• On iPhone a new document’s Before and After control is dimmed as a whole, as iOS dims a control it turns off; deciding lands at once and the review closes.

Not drawn yet: the design menu in the iPhone picker sheet.

design-panels.text:
For approval: each panel on the canvas closes on its own

The canvas can have three columns beside it: the app’s sidebar, the left panel (pages and layers) and the right panel (edit and comments). Until now one button hid both panels together, so a review in a normal window was cramped.

• The button at the top of the left panel is now Hide left panel. The right panel gets its own Hide right panel button at the end of its top row.
• A closed panel leaves one small button at that top corner of the canvas to bring it back. The review bar, the tools and the frames stay where they are and the canvas takes the room.
• Each panel’s state is remembered on this device, separately, like the app sidebar’s. Opening a review never changes them.
• The app sidebar keeps its own Collapse button and ⌘\. Below 820 px nothing changes: the left panel is already folded and the right one is a sheet.

packages-kept.text: Everything kept, other states. Kind filter: one button, "npm and Cargo", opens a menu with both ticked; search always covers what is ticked. Untick one and the button reads "npm only" or "Cargo only"; the last ticked kind can’t be unticked. Empty: "Nothing kept yet. The first install through deploy.local appears here." No match: "No package or crate matches left-pad" with Clear. Nothing idle: the Copies row reads "Everything was installed in the last 30 days" with no chevron. Loading: the count line reads "Counting…". After removing: a notice, "Removed 1.9 GB. 4.3 GB kept." While a source is unreachable the removal dialog adds that removed packages can’t be fetched again until it’s back. Cargo: every kept crate reads "Needed by projects", is never listed under Not installed in 30 days and is never cleaned up, until deploy.local reads Cargo.lock. Counts of one read "1 version" and "1 package". iPhone: the same three pages as pushed screens from Packages › Copies, search in the navigation bar, filters as a menu.

project-first-rules.text: Project-first proposal. A piece of work is one row with a stage: Up next (what you wrote down), Found by agents (waiting for you to accept or dismiss), Running, Needs you, Shipped. A project’s Work tab lists them and takes the place of Issues and Pull requests; a pull request is part of its work item. The sidebar’s Work setting keeps Agents where they are and replaces the dated task list with projects that have live work, each row with its state; agent runs stay with their agent, and work with no project sits under Chats. Work can belong to several projects: a change to a package you own shows as the same row in each project that uses what changed, and each project merges its own update when it chooses. What uses what comes from a code index built on every push, and the index is the only source for it. A project’s Graph tab draws one section per kind of connection the index reports, so a new indexer adds a section without changing the other pages; search and agent findings read the same index. Existing boards keep the date sidebar until this is approved.

diagnostics-how.text:
Proposal. A way to debug deploy.local from inside deploy.local: git activity, the health of its own processes, its own API timings, its server log and a CPU profiler, in one place.

• Where: Computers → Diagnostics, beside deploy.local updates, and the deploy.local row under Runs on SER’s page opens it. It is about the server, not a project, and it is the same kind of page as updates. No sidebar entry.
• Only admins: non-admins see neither the button nor the row, and the API refuses them, as the profiler API already does.
• Tabs: Overview, Git, Processes, API requests, Logs, Profiler. Overview says in one line whether anything needs a look, then one row per part with a dot and a label. A problem gets a warning banner that names the cause it can see and one next step.
• States: calm (most days), attention, and a new server where each part fills in as it happens. A tab with nothing yet uses the empty pattern: “No git activity yet. Pushes, fetches and clones show here.”
• Nothing here changes how deploy.local runs. Recording a profile is the only action.

diagnostics-overview-how.text:
When Overview warns
• Git: a push, fetch or clone over 10 s, or any failure. More than 3 slow in an hour, or 2 failures in a row to one repository, raise a banner.
• Processes: event-loop p99 over 200 ms or a longest pause over 1 s (the supervisor’s existing log threshold), held for 3 minutes; any restart that was not an update.
• API requests: requests over 1 s, against the route’s own usual time.
• Logs: errors in the last hour.
A banner clears on its own once the cause has been normal for 10 minutes. Earlier this week keeps the last 7 days of them.

diagnostics-git-how.text:
Git, what is recorded (new; nothing is recorded today)
• Every push, fetch and clone over HTTPS and SSH: repository, operation, protocol, who (person and computer, or the task or checks behind it), bytes each way, time, git’s exit code and its last lines of output.
• For a push, time is split at what the server can see: signing in, receiving the upload, git storing it, starting checks. That separates a slow network or a stalled control from slow git.
• Background work (import, fetch, sync, merge a pull request, set up a task’s copy) adds Waited to the timestamps it already keeps, so a task that starts late shows what it queued behind.
• Slow means over 10 s. At the same time on SER links the process, background work and API numbers from that minute.
• Kept 90 days, like request logs.

diagnostics-traffic-how.text:
Traffic (added to the Diagnostics proposal; for approval)
• Why: six scripts left running on MacBook Pro fetched forma’s front page every two seconds for five days, 242,000 requests a day, and nothing said so. Each request is already kept with its address and agent; nobody was looking at who sends them.
• Traffic is a seventh tab: requests through deploy.local to every app and to deploy.local itself, a minute-by-minute line, the repeating senders, and each app with its busiest sender.
• A repeating sender is one address that sent at least 80% of one route’s requests and at least 1,000 of them, at a steady pace, for over an hour. Steady means the gaps between requests barely vary, which is what a loop looks like and a person or a browser does not.
• The address is named when it belongs to one of your computers (“MacBook Pro”); otherwise it shows as the address.
• Where it shows: a warning on Traffic, the Traffic row on Overview turns to “Repeating”, and the app’s own Requests page gets the same warning with “Leave it out”, which hides that sender from the page’s numbers until you turn it back.
• It goes to Waiting on you once it has lasted a day. It clears on its own an hour after the sender stops.
• New to record: requests to deploy.local’s own pages by sender. App requests are already kept for 90 days.
• Not here: blocking a sender. This says who and what; stopping it is yours.

diagnostics-processes-how.text:
Processes and API requests
• The supervisor already samples each process every minute (event-loop p50, p99, max, RSS, heap) but keeps only the latest. Keep every sample for 30 days, like resource metrics, and record each exit with its code or signal and whether it was an update, a crash or a missed heartbeat.
• The charts show one process at a time; the 200 ms line is the existing warning threshold. These are the only charts, because here the trend is the point: is it new, and is memory climbing.
• API requests: always on, per route (ids grouped as :id), the timing the profiler collects today. Event streams and git routes are left out. Kept 30 days; each request over 1 s is kept by itself for 30 days with who sent it and its status.

diagnostics-profiler-how.text:
Logs and profiler
• Logs reads the supervisor’s server log on SER (20 MB, plus three rotated copies), the same lines as today, with filters by process, level and time, live while open. Download gives the file.
• Profiler uses the existing admin API: control only, 1–120 seconds (offered as 10 s, 30 s, 1 min, 2 min), one at a time. A second admin sees Recording… with who started it.
• New: each result is kept for 30 days, so it can be opened after leaving the page and shared. Download .cpuprofile gives the raw profile for Chrome DevTools or speedscope.
• Own time and Including what it calls are the summary’s self and inclusive lists; Requests while recording is its route list.

project-work-empty.text:
The other empty lines on Work

• Shipped with nothing in it: “Nothing shipped yet” with “Merged pull requests, finished tasks and closed ideas show here.” No actions.

design-commands.text:
A design worked on outside a task
CliDesign.html and CliDesignReview.html are the commands: start, check, propose, feedback, resolve. After Ask for changes the review bar names who has the notes: a task, a terminal that was waiting (DesignReviewCanvasTerminal.html), or nobody (DesignReviewCanvasNoOne.html), which offers Start a task. An approval that main overtakes says Did not reach main and asks again (DesignReviewCanvasNotLanded.html); it never reads on main. Once a design is on main its branch is removed, and the canvas says it shows main (DesignReviewCanvasApproved.html).

pull-request-states.text:
An open pull request no task opened. The decision comes first, in one row under the title: what stands in the way in plain words, then its actions. Merge and Close are the same actions the task page uses, and the reasons are the server's mergeBlock wording. The other states, as the row's line and its actions:
• Checks still running: “Checks running · Required pipeline checks have not passed for 8ab72bd yet: 2 of 4 done.” Close, Merge disabled until they pass.
• A required check failed: “Checks failed · Required pipeline checks have not passed for 8ab72bd: test failed.” test links to its run. Close, Fix in a task (primary), which starts a task on build/project-work with the failed run.
• Nothing to merge: “Nothing to merge · build/project-work has no commits that main does not already have.” Close (primary).
• Merging: “Merging into main…” with a spinner. No actions until it lands or fails.
• Merge failed: “Merge failed · <the server's error>”. Close, Retry merge (primary).
• Closed: the pill reads Closed, the row reads “Closed · Gabriel closed this pull request <when>.” Reopen (secondary).
• Merged: after Merge succeeds the page becomes PullRequest.html: the Merged row in the first group says what happened, and there is no decision row.

Close asks nothing; Reopen undoes it. Merge asks nothing more than the task page's Merge only: it merges into main at once.

Conflicts: the line is conflictReason()'s first sentence. Its second sentence (“Ask the task to merge main into its branch…”) is for task pull requests; with no task the action says it instead: Update from main in a task starts a task on build/project-work asked to merge main and resolve those files.

⋯ beside the title holds Start a task on this branch (open) or Start a follow-up task on main (merged or closed); it replaces the old notice and its Follow up in a task button. On these pages the header's New task is secondary so Merge is the one primary action.

Files: all folded, path order, eight then Show 60 more; Filter files narrows by path (PullRequestBlocked shows it filtered). An opened image shows a preview with its size; an opened text file shows its diff as on PullRequest. Merges from main fold into one line that opens to list them.
